passages.happening:
Israel goes north on the road to Bashan, and its king, Og, comes out with his whole army to fight at Edrei (verse 1). God says to Moses, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land” (verse 2).

Israel defeats him and takes all sixty of his cities, ‘fortified with high walls and gates and bars’ (verse 5). “We devoted them to destruction, as we had done to Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children of every city” (verse 6). The livestock and plunder were kept (verse 7).

Moses sums up what Israel now holds: all the land east of the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley in the south to Mount Hermon in the north (verses 8-10). A note is added about Og himself. He was the last of the Rephaim, and his bed of iron, ‘nine cubits long and four cubits wide’, could still be seen in Rabbah of the Ammonites (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Bashan was the high, well-watered plateau east of the Sea of Galilee. The Bible remembers it elsewhere for its cattle and its oak trees. Edrei is usually identified with the modern town of Daraa in southern Syria.

A hearer who knew the story of Kadesh would catch the point of the details. Forty years earlier Israel had refused the land because the cities were walled and the people tall. Here are sixty walled cities, and a king from the giants of old. The Rephaim were a people of the land's far past, remembered as huge and fearsome. Og is the last of them. The thing the parents said could not be done, the children have just watched God do.

The bed measured about thirteen feet by six. A cubit was the length of a forearm, about eighteen inches. Some take it as a real bed, a showpiece of a king's size and wealth at a time when iron was precious. Others think it was a burial couch or a stone coffin of the dark basalt of that region. The text does not settle it. The remark that it ‘is still in Rabbah’ reads like a note from a later hand, written for readers who could go and look.

Verse 6 uses the hardest word in these chapters again. To ‘devote to destruction’ was to give a conquered town over wholly, so that its people were not kept as slaves. Israel was not the only nation to do this. A Moabite king named Mesha, in the ninth century BC, boasted on his monument that he had done the same to an Israelite town in the name of his own god. Here, as with Sihon, the verse says plainly who was killed: ‘the men, women, and children of every city’. The hard question on chapter 2, verses 24 to 37, sets out how Christians have read this, and what follows below adds to it.
passages.later:
Numbers tells the same battle in three verses, with the same word from God: “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand” (Numbers 21:34).

Israel remembered the two kings together in its songs: “Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kings of Canaan” (Psalm 135:11).

The New Testament gives the church no land to take and no people to fight. Paul writes, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
passages.hard:
The chapter says Israel destroyed ‘the men, women, and children of every city’. How can that be in the Bible?

A reader is right to be troubled. Christians who take the text seriously have answered in several ways.

Some stress that the conquest is presented as a single act of God's judgment on peoples whose wickedness he had long put up with. God told Abraham that ‘the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete’ (Genesis 15:16). On this reading it is not a pattern for any later war, and chapter 20 limits it to the land itself.

Some hold that the language of total destruction was the usual way of reporting a victory in the ancient world, as the inscription of Mesha shows. They note that the books of Joshua and Judges report Canaanites still living in the land long afterward. On this reading the words overstate what happened, as such reports commonly did.

Others hold that these texts show God meeting Israel within its world, while leading his people toward the fuller teaching of love for enemies in Christ. Those who object say this weakens the authority of Scripture.

None of these answers removes the difficulty, and readers differ over which carries most weight. These notes take no side.

On one point Christians agree. No one may appeal to these chapters to justify violence against any person or people. They speak of kingdoms that passed away long ago and say nothing about any nation or conflict today.

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: The new generation saw the very thing their parents had feared, and saw that God was greater. Ask what fear was handed down to you, and whether you have ever tested it against what God has done. And when you read verse 6, do not look away. Ask God the question Abraham asked him, and keep reading.

passages.t: The land east of the river, and a word for Joshua
passages.happening:
Moses gives the conquered land to two and a half tribes. Reuben and Gad receive the south, from the Arnon up into Gilead. Half of the tribe of Manasseh receives the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan (verses 12-17).

There is a condition. “All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites” (verse 18). Their wives, children and livestock may stay in the towns, ‘until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you’ (verse 20). Then they may go home.

Moses then speaks to Joshua. “Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. The LORD will do the same to all the kingdoms you are about to enter. Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you” (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
Numbers 32 tells how this came about. Reuben and Gad had large herds, saw good grazing east of the Jordan, and asked to settle there. Moses feared they meant to leave the other tribes to fight alone. They promised to go over first.

Land in Israel was held by clans and handed down inside them. That is why a man named Jair can give his own name to a group of villages (verse 14).

The condition is the heart of the passage. These tribes already have what the others are still waiting for. They have homes, fields and safety. Moses will not let them settle into it while their brothers are still at risk. They must go in front, and they may not rest until the others can.

The word ‘rest’ matters in this book. It means a settled, secure life in the land, free from enemies. It becomes one of the great words of hope in the Bible.

The charge to Joshua looks back in order to look forward. Joshua has seen two kings fall. What God has done is the ground for trusting what God will do. Moses does not tell Joshua that he is able. He tells him that God will fight.
passages.later:
Joshua released these tribes years later in the same words: “And now that the LORD your God has given your brothers rest as He promised them, you may return to your homes” (Joshua 22:4).

The letter to the Hebrews says that the rest Joshua gave was not the end of the promise: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day. There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8-9).
passages.asks: The tribes that were already safe had to go first for those who were not. Ask who is still waiting for what you already have, whether safety, a home or a settled life, and what it would mean for you to go ahead of them. And notice what Moses gives Joshua for courage. Ask what you have already seen God do that could steady you for what is coming.

passages.happening:
Moses now tells the people about a prayer of his own. “At that time I also pleaded with the LORD” (verse 23). He praised God for what he had begun to show, and then he asked: “Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan” (verse 25).

“But the LORD was angry with me on account of you, and He would not listen to me. ‘That is enough,’ the LORD said to me. ‘Do not speak to Me again about this matter’” (verse 26).

Moses is told to climb to the top of Pisgah and look in every direction. “See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan” (verse 27). He is to prepare Joshua: ‘encourage him, and strengthen him, for he will cross over ahead of the people’ (verse 28).

“So we stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter has narrowed step by step: from the armies, to the tribes, to Joshua, and now to one old man praying alone.

Two words have run through the whole chapter, ‘cross over’ and ‘see’. The fighting men must cross. Joshua has seen. Moses asks to cross and see. He is allowed only to see.

His prayer is humble. He calls himself God's servant. He says God has only ‘begun’ to show his greatness, and he longs to see the rest. He has led this people for forty years toward one place, and he asks to set foot in it.

God's answer is short and final. He is not cruel to Moses. He is firm, and then at once he gives him two things: a view of the whole land, and a task. Moses is to put courage into the man who will finish what he began. The Hebrew verb for ‘strengthen’ becomes the refrain of Joshua's calling: be strong and courageous.

Moses says the LORD was angry with him ‘on account of you’. The note on chapter 1, verses 34 to 46, sets out how readers understand this beside Numbers 20, where Moses' own failure at the rock is the reason.

Why does Moses tell the people this at all? He is about to ask them for a lifetime of obedience. He lets them see that he himself has asked God for something with all his heart and been told no, and that he is still here, still serving, still calling God good.

The valley where the scene ends lies opposite Beth-peor, the place where Israel had fallen into idol worship not long before. The next chapter begins there.
passages.later:
The book returns to this at its end, when Moses climbs the mountain: ‘I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it’ (Deuteronomy 34:4).

Paul tells of a prayer of his own that was refused: “Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me. But He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:8-9).

Jesus himself prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39).

And Moses did stand in the land at last. On a mountain there, in the days of Jesus, “Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared before them, talking with Jesus” (Matthew 17:3).
passages.asks: Moses asked for the one thing he most wanted and was told no. He did not stop serving. Ask what you have pleaded for and not been given, and what you have done with God since. And look at the task God gave Moses in place of his wish. Ask whether there is someone you are meant to strengthen for work you will not see finished.
